case_name: Regular monthly transaction — 48 equal payments, regular first period
appendix_basis: 12 CFR 1026, Appendix J(b) (section letter per best recall) — actuarial-method equation A + Σ_i P_i(1+I)^(-t_i) = 0, unit-period = 1 month → 12 unit-periods per year, APR = 100 × I × 12 (nominal annualization). The equation/unit-period machinery is Appendix J's; the numeric values below are constructed, not reproduced from Appendix J.

inputs.payment_schedule: 48 monthly payments of USD 263.34, first due exactly 1 month after the advance (regular first period)

unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = interval between contractual payment dates = 1 month; 12 unit-periods per year. All intervals regular, so t_i = i (1…48), measured in unit-periods from the advance; no fractional unit-periods arise. I = unit-period (monthly) rate; APR = 100 × I × 12, i.e. nominal annualization, not (1+I)^12 − 1.
weakest_point: Whether Appendix J itself prescribes a final rounding step (nearest 1/8 of 1 percentage point) versus leaving accuracy to the §1026.22 tolerances — I state both; the actuarial equation, 12 unit-periods/year for monthly, and nominal annualization (APR = 12 × I) I am confident of; the 10,000 / 48 × 263.34 numbers are mine.

case_name: Irregular (short) first period with odd days — 12 monthly payments
appendix_basis: Appendix J(c) irregular-transaction rules (section letter per best recall) — an irregular first period is counted in days and expressed as a fractional unit-period (days in the fractional period ÷ days in the unit-period), which enters the exponent t directly. Rule content recalled; numeric example constructed.

inputs.payment_schedule: 12 payments of USD 88.56 on the 5th of each month; advance Jan 15 → first payment Feb 5 (21 days after advance), last payment Jan 5 of the following year

unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month, 12 per year. The 21-day first interval is SHORTER than a unit-period → the first period is a fractional unit-period: 21 days ÷ 31 days (actual days in the corresponding full period Jan 15→Feb 15) = 0.6774194. Exponents: t_i = 0.6774194 + (i−1) → 0.6774, 1.6774, 2.6774, …, 11.6774. Later intervals (Feb 5→Mar 5 etc.) remain 1 unit-period each even though their day counts vary (28/31) — unit-periods are contractual intervals, not day counts; only the odd days are converted to a fraction.
result_apr: 12.0000% on the exact payment (88.5640); 11.9908% after cents-rounding to 88.56 → disclosed 12.000% under nearest-1/8 rounding (two-decimal rounding would print 11.99%)
weakest_point: The day-count basis for the fractional unit-period: I used 21 ÷ 31 (actual days of the corresponding full month); if Appendix J prescribes a standardized divisor (e.g., 30 days → t₁ = 0.70), the payment shifts ~2¢ and the APR a few bp, and for LONG first periods the choice matters more — I cannot certify the exact basis, nor that this numeric example is published.

appendix_basis: Appendix J definitions of 'unit-period' and 'number of unit-periods per year' plus its single-payment instructions (section letter uncertain to me) — recalled rule: with a single payment date the unit-period is the advance-to-payment interval, and for non-standard intervals the per-year count = 365 ÷ days in the unit-period. Numeric example constructed.

inputs.payment_schedule: single payment of USD 1,100.00 due 182 days after the advance

unit_period_analysis: No recurring contractual payment dates → per the recalled single-payment rule the unit-period is the entire advance-to-payment interval (182 days), so t = 1 exactly and no fractional-unit-period question arises. Unit-periods per year = 365 ÷ 182 = 2.0054945. APR = 100 × I × 2.0054945.
computation:
Step 1 — Equation: 1,000 × (1+I)^1 = 1,100 (Appendix J sign form: 1,000 + 1,100×(1+I)^(-1) = 0).
Step 2 — Closed form, no iteration: (1+I) = 1,100/1,000 = 1.100000 → I = 0.100000 per 182-day unit-period.
Step 3 — Annualization count: 365 ÷ 182 = 2.0054945.
Step 4 — APR = 0.100000 × 2.0054945 = 0.2005495 → 20.0549%.
Step 5 — Contrast showing the unit-period definition drives the answer: if the note were instead measured in monthly unit-periods (t = 6), I = 1.10^(1/6) − 1 = 1.6012%/month → APR = 12 × 1.6012% = 19.2142%.
weakest_point: Direction-of-rule risk on the unit-period definition: my recall is that a single-payment transaction's unit-period spans the whole advance-to-payment term (corroborated by payday-style APRs = fee% × 365/term, e.g. 15 per 100 over 14 days → 391.07%); if that is wrong and t is measured in months, the answer is 19.21% not 20.05%. Also unsure the divisor is exactly 365 ÷ days (leap-year handling unknown).

case_name: Irregular payment amounts — 11 level payments plus a balloon
appendix_basis: Appendix J(b) actuarial equation with payment-specific P_i — unequal amounts are handled by summing each P_i at its own exponent t_i. Numeric example constructed (balloon back-solved from a 12% target); does not reproduce any published Appendix J figures.

inputs.payment_schedule: months 1–11: USD 500.00 each; month 12: USD 5,427.00 (balloon); regular monthly intervals, regular first period

unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month, 12 per year; timing is regular so t_i = i (1…12). The irregularity is in the AMOUNTS P_i, which the equation accommodates by summing each payment at its own exponent. No fractional unit-periods.
weakest_point: The measurement point of t_i — Appendix J's phrasing may be 'from the beginning of the first payment period' rather than 'from the advance'; identical here only because the first period is regular. The balloon was back-solved from a 12% target, so the example verifies by construction rather than reproducing a published figure.

case_name: Irregular payment schedule — skipped month 6 (deferred payment)
appendix_basis: Appendix J(b)/(c): exponents t_i count ELAPSED unit-periods from the advance, so a gap in the schedule is carried in t, not in payment numbering. Rule content recalled; numeric example constructed (payment back-solved from a 12% target).

inputs.payment_schedule: 11 payments of USD 969.65 due at months 1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10,11,12 — no payment due in month 6 per the original contract; regular first period

unit_period_analysis: Unit-period = 1 month, 12 per year; t_i counts elapsed unit-periods from the advance, so payments after the gap carry t = 7…12 even though they are only the 6th–11th payments made. Exponent set: {1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10,11,12}. No fractional periods (regular first period).
weakest_point: I assume the month-6 gap is part of the ORIGINAL contractual schedule, so the t_i framework applies unchanged; if the deferral arose from a later modification/forbearance, the original-schedule premise — and possibly the amount financed — would differ. The time-based exponent treatment itself I am confident of.
